### 1. Cache Engineering for Agents (2610.28577)
- what: Proposes "cache engineering," where an agent drops selected KV entries from attention (`drop`) and re-rotates retained keys' RoPE positions (`repos`) without rewriting the text or re-prefilling, and builds the AKV serving engine (extended radix tree, drop-aware eviction, segment-batch attention) to support it.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: Tool-response rolling drop (keep latest 12 tool rounds) vs. Standard summarization at 96K: average cost 27.7% lower (5.0→... averaged over 3 models × 4 benchmarks, Table 1); average score +1.3–2.1 pts per model (paper's own text). Serving: 1.18× output throughput and 1.51× P95 latency gain on GPT-OSS-120B, Top-80 SWE-Verified, 8×A800 BF16. Ablation: `repos` raises BCP score 55→62 on GPT-OSS-120B (single 100-task subset).
- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV). No weights needed; built on SGLang v0.5.20.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The cheap, testable idea is the tool-response rolling-drop policy and the `repos` ablation, and both can be tried on an agent harness that exposes KV control, which an API-only setup like Muninn's cannot. The headline gains rest on one model family and 100-task subsets, several reported deltas are a few points (single runs or small subsets, with error bars shown only for the SWE online plot), and the cost numbers use Groq/MiniMax list prices with a self-chosen cache-hit rate for `repos`, so treat the 27.7% as a claim to verify rather than a planning number. The real barrier is that AKV needs a server you control to run `drop`/`repos`; a hosted API user can only take the design lesson that tool outputs decay in attention and that trimming should be incremental, not abrupt.

### 1. LiFT: Loop Flow Transformers (2610.05538)
- what: Trains a looped DiT core where each loop is supervised at a point on a straight path from the initial velocity estimate to the flow-matching target, then lets inference loop count be raised beyond training depth to trade compute for quality.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no URL was given, and the paper's own arXiv id is 2610.05538) / abstract / none — read in full from the supplied text.
- key numbers: L/2 R10 goes from FID 20.30 at 2 training loops to 10.95 at 8 inference loops (50 steps). With 25 steps and 4 loops it hits FID 13.16 at 7.40 TFLOPs, versus dense L/2 at 16.94 and 8.07 TFLOPs (50 steps). Dense L/2 needs 250 steps to reach 15.74; LiFT is about 41% smaller in parameters.
- code/weights: not stated. The paper's front matter shows "Coming Soon" placeholders, and I found no repository or checkpoint link in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism is a training change for a looped DiT, so reproducing it means training from scratch on ImageNet at 4 H100s for 500k updates, which the profile puts out of reach. The inference-side finding is the useful part: a fixed checkpoint can add loops at test time, and at B/2 the dense model still wins. Every result is a single run on class-conditional ImageNet without CFG, and the paper says so, so the gains are not yet shown for text or guided generation.

### 1. Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement (2610.12369)
- what: Proposes Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP), a frozen, model-free robot policy written as a shared code library with explicit perception/state, which coding agents iteratively improve offline on RoboDojo's 42 bimanual tasks.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, rated from the supplied paper text)
- key numbers: 70.24% overall SR on RoboDojo vs 31.38% for the best leaderboard entry (PhysicalRSI, agent+VLA); Memory 89.9% and Precision 75.1%; control step median 0.3 ms on CPU. Test-set SR 74.9% vs validation 76.7% on standard layouts, but randomized layouts drop to 52.8–54.1%.
- code/weights: not stated (no repository, code release, or weights link appears in the paper text).
- practical: LOW
- why: The result is a simulation-only benchmark number, and the policy depends on hand-written perception using benchmark-published camera models, meshes and object sizes, which the authors themselves call a major limitation. Nothing is released, so it cannot be replicated in weeks; the transferable idea is narrow: a design rule that offline coding-agent loops with accept-only-if-no-regression gates (Eq. 3 and 5) can improve a deterministic controller, which may matter for the Claude Code harness and skill-testing workflow. The paper's own randomized-layout numbers (~53–54% vs 77% standard) show the gap that matters for your use.

### 1. Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World (arXiv 2610.14224)
- what: Proposes a plug-and-play framework that refines an agent's execution harness per task via a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step (parallel or sequential recursion), and updates a separate improvement-harness library after each task so later harness edits get better.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no URL was fetched, and the paper's own GitHub link is github.com/google-research/harness2)
- key numbers: With Gemini 3.5 Flash under OpenCode, WorkBuddy-Bench Avg. goes from 72.4 (base) to 77.5 (one step, k=1) and 80.8 at k=5; the library ablation drops WorkBuddy from 77.5 to 74.4 and JobBench from 36.0 to 34.2. Gains are on a single LAB stream of 100 tasks with 3 runs each.
- code/weights: the paper links github.com/google-research/harness2 and harness2.github.io. No model weights are released (the executors are commercial APIs).
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The reusable pieces are the contrastive probe-then-compose loop and the rule that each task's edits go into a library of executable components plus an EXPERIENCE.md, which you could replicate on your own Muninn skills/hooks setup within weeks. It is weaker for your routing and cost work: the step multiplies executions (k=5 gives 5 probes plus 5 compositions per task), the "no ground truth" claim rests on an LLM editor (Claude Opus 4.8) judging its own evidence, and the headline gains are 1–4 points on several cells with a sd of 1–5 over only 3 runs.

### 1. Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation (2610.14162)
- what: Trains a multiscale residual VQ-VAE to turn text into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of discrete codes, then a ~100M transformer generates each level in parallel, so generation takes about K≈8–32 sequential steps instead of many denoising passes.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was fetched, and the paper's own GitHub link is https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm)
- key numbers: LM1B: 11× fewer NFE than DUO and 21× faster wall-clock at better Gen. PPL (93.05 vs 97.30 for DUO at 128 NFE, using 12 NFE); XSum: ROUGE-L 28.0 at 8 NFE vs AURORA-LM 26.6 at 128 NFE; Sudoku hard 86.1% vs FMLM+ 81.3%.
- code/weights: GitHub repo linked (https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm); weights release not explicitly stated in the text I read.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The decode-cost idea (few sequential steps, short coarse sequences, one forward pass per level) is directly transferable to any cheap-generator routing setup, and the ~4–5× lower training-token budget is a useful data point. However, every headline number rests on ~100M-parameter generators trained for 50k–350k steps on a single H100-class budget, and the baselines are mostly the authors' own reruns or other papers' checkpoints, so replicating the 21× speedup claim would take real GPU time, not weeks of a laptop-scale test.

### 1. TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing (2610.12242)
- what: Serving system (built on SGLang 0.5.1) that runs each LLM in a routed set as a subserver, with a route/send/receive API, handoff-resume for routed requests, and a delayed-batching scheduler whose threshold is chosen from a DTMC throughput model.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched). Code link is taken from the abstract.
- key numbers: 2.01–64.15× decoding throughput over existing implementations across 15 algorithm/workload combinations; at concurrency 4 on R2R original settings, 89.62 → 244.56 tok/s vs. official code, and 145.30 tok/s for the LLM-only baseline. Ablation at N=8: 132.78 (no optimisations) → 372.48 tok/s. Throughput gain on the SLM–LLM pair ablation is 1.99–3.21× over official R2R.
- code/weights: GitHub link stated in the abstract (github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter). Model weights are the public Qwen3 models; no separate release stated.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: If you run token-level routing across a local small/large model pair, the handoff-resume idea (keep KV state across model switches instead of re-running prefix matching) and the delayed-batch threshold are concrete design changes you could copy into a scheduler. The headline 64× is against weak baselines (official CITER/Co-LLM code with no continuous batching, and a dispatcher-based Std. Serving that the authors built), so expect much smaller gains against a well-tuned vLLM/SGLang setup. The approach only fits if your routing is per-token and both models are on hardware you control; for Muninn's API-level delegation to cheaper models it doesn't apply.

- what: Converts 100k anonymized social-platform user behavior histories into 75k predictive/rubric-scored training tasks, then SFTs Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on the resulting trajectories and runs GSPO on top.

- key numbers: VelaBench 51.5 → 63.0 (+11.5) for the base vs. Vela-35B-A3B; general OOD average +4.0 (58.2 vs 54.2); RL-from-SFT vs RL-from-base +7.7 on VelaBench (66.2 vs 58.5). - code/weights: repo link stated (github.com/AllSpark-Research/Vela); the paper says code, templates and prompts "will be" released, so the stated link may not yet contain them. Weights: not stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: The data is proprietary platform behavior logs, and the pipeline depends on a 2.4T-parameter model for composing and scoring, which makes it hard to replicate in weeks. The one transferable idea is the filter: keep tasks where a model's mean score sits in [0.2, 0.8] and accept a trajectory only if it beats that mean; this is cheap to borrow for your own eval or routing data. ### 1. Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To (arXiv 2610.11765)
- what: Defines "no-thinking" as a response-level property and measures it with three metrics (Empty-Thinking Rate, instruction-aware relevance QRel., and an LLM-judge Explicit Inference Rate) across six models, six benchmarks, and six prompt/thinking-control modes.

- key numbers: Open-ended tasks under strict answer-only prompting (M5) keep EIR at 62.00% (GPT-5.5 judge; Claude Opus 4.8 gives 61.02%), versus 99.69% under native Think-Off (M2). - code/weights: not stated in the paper text. It mentions "evaluation artifacts" containing per-example annotations and fixed sample IDs, but gives no repository or release link.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The most useful design finding is that answer-space shape (Bool < MCQ < Open) predicts how much visible reasoning leaks, and that Bool and candidate-visible framings compress answers cheaply at flat accuracy. ### 1. RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models (arXiv 2610.13912)
- what: Proposes a domain-general loop in which a JEPA-style world model ranks candidate actions before external execution, feedback updates the policy/workflow and optionally the world model, and component plus pair-compatibility checks decide which policy–model pair is kept.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was fetched, and the paper's own GitHub/HF links are listed as stated)
- key numbers: Code repair hidden-test success 26.3% (static verifier) → 29.2% (fixed world-model selection, paired gain +2.83 pp, 95% CI [+0.17, +5.50]) → 31.2% (with world-model adaptation), all at ~3.72 online test calls/task. Reaction optimization 96.15% vs 82.16% for Bayesian optimization at 40 experiments (single flow LC–MS screen). GUI checkbox success 51% → 99% with 39.4% fewer actions.
- code/weights: Code link https://github.com/Gen-Verse/RSI-Anything; the "Models" link points to a Hugging Face *dataset* page (huggingface.co/datasets/Gen-Verse/RSI-Anything), so it is unclear whether model weights are released. The paper does not give a separate weights link.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism is a reasonable pattern (rank N candidates with a cheap predictor, run only the best one, log prediction vs. outcome), and that pattern is directly usable for routing or gating. But the headline gains are small on the code-repair side (≈+2.8 pp over a static verifier, one benchmark, one fixed coder), and the reaction result is one screen against Bayesian optimization, with no variance reported. The "recursive" claim rests on about three update cycles and does not show sustained mutual improvement, which the authors themselves say is still needed. The one transferable idea is the version-tagged reliability check: only score a predictor on predictions made by the current model version, and treat insufficient coverage as "unknown," not "reliable."

### 1. Meta² : Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents (2611.05139)
- what: Learns an offline textual "Meta-Skill" from A/B/C rollout contrasts (no evolver / evolver guided by the current Meta-Skill / evolver with verifier access), then freezes it and uses it to guide KEEP-or-EVOLVE decisions at checkpoints inside each run, with edits discarded when the run ends.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, only the project page https://meta-square.github.io/ listed in the header) — the full text was supplied, so this is a full read.
- key numbers: Terminal-Bench 2.1 with GPT-5.6-Terra: 81.00% vs NexAU seed 66.33% and best baseline Meta-Harness 73.33%. DeepSWE 1.1: 44.44% vs seed 34.67% and Meta-Harness 37.33%. Ablation on Terminal-Bench: online evolver with no knowledge 74.67%, self-distilled Meta-Skill 77.00%, contrastive Meta-Skill 81.00%. Both benchmarks are small (60 and 75 test tasks), with reported SDs of about 0.9 and 0.8 points on the Meta² rows. Per-run SD is about 4 to 5 points on most baselines, so single-point gaps of a few points are weak evidence.
- code/weights: not stated in the paper. The only link is the project page https://meta-square.github.io/. No repo or Meta-Skill release is mentioned.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The reusable idea is concrete and testable: a frozen, entry-structured "act / hold / avoid" guidance file, consulted at checkpoints, with per-run harness edits that reset between tasks. - what: Describes CoworkOS, a harness that splits a Main agent (decides strategy, delegation, acceptance) from a runtime Coordinator that runs async Subagents, shared revisioned app resources (docs, PPTist, CAD, Blender), hierarchical workspaces, and Jobs/semantic memory for resumable long-horizon work, then reports benchmark scores and a five-round automated post-training run.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched). Repo, project page and showcase are listed in the paper, but I did not open them.
- key numbers: Tool-use/productivity/search/ML-coding averages of 55.22/57.54/82.14/56.26 vs DSH 55.31/56.13/76.64/56.14 and OpenHands 51.33/55.27/82.22/44.66 (Table 1, single-run, GLM-5.3 backbone for all harnesses). Post-training: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B avg over 8 benchmarks 33.19 → 42.95 across five rounds (Table 2). Baselines are other harnesses on the same model, not other agent frameworks on tuned settings.
- code/weights: Repo github.com/RUC-NLPIR/CoworkOS and project page coworkos-ai.github.io are stated. Whether the harness and training data/checkpoints are released under those links is not confirmed in the text.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The reusable pieces are concrete: a per-resource revision check (`Commit` on base revision, returning conflict instead of overwriting) and a context-reconstruction rule (memory doc plus runtime projection on reset).
